items.title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
items.tldr: Microsoft issued a public apology after a technical glitch during a network upgrade knocked out Outlook, Teams and other essential services for roughly 24 hours, impacting over 70 countries and more than 430 million users. The incident highlighted the fragile dependence of governments, hospitals, schools and businesses on a handful of cloud providers, prompting fresh debate over infrastructure resilience and regulatory oversight.
items.background: The outage, which began on Thursday and largely recovered by Friday afternoon, was traced to a network capacity upgrade that introduced an unexpected configuration error. Microsoft described the problem as a non‑cyber, non‑AI‑related technical fault, but the scale of the disruption—spanning the Japanese government, the Philippines Supreme Court, the UK NHS, North American rail systems and countless private enterprises—underscored how modern critical services are built on a narrow ecosystem of big‑tech platforms. Analysts refer to such events as "single points of failure" that can cascade across economies, prompting calls for diversified redundancy and clearer regulatory frameworks for digital essential services.

analysis.heading: Technical Timeline and Root‑Cause Assessment
analysis.content: Microsoft first detected the issue at 17:54 GMT on Thursday when Exchange Online mailboxes in the Americas became inaccessible. Within hours the fault propagated globally, reaching a peak impact by early Friday when only partial recoveries were reported in North America and Europe. By 13:32 GMT the company announced broader improvements, noting that the gradual restoration was intentional to maintain service stability. The company’s internal investigation identified the outage as a mis‑configuration introduced during a routine network capacity upgrade, ruling out ransomware, AI‑driven attacks or external sabotage. The incident illustrates how even carefully scripted infrastructure changes can trigger widespread service failures when insufficient rollback mechanisms or real‑time monitoring are in place.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Economic Ripple Effects
analysis.content: The outage’s reach into sovereign functions—Japanese ministries, Philippine judicial bodies, Singapore’s government portals, and UK NHS trusts—demonstrated that digital infrastructure has become a de‑facto public utility. In Canada, rail operators could not send email updates to passengers, while U.S. House of Representatives staff reported a full day of legislative work lost because all communications ran on Microsoft Outlook. Smaller entities, such as South African winemaker Peter Pentz, described their operations grinding to a halt, emphasizing the disproportionate impact on firms that lack robust backup systems. The event has intensified diplomatic conversations about technology sovereignty, with several nations revisiting strategies to reduce reliance on a single vendor for essential services.

analysis.heading: Policy Implications and Regulatory Outlook
analysis.content: Regulators are now weighing whether cloud services that underpin critical infrastructure should be subject to stricter oversight akin to utilities. The UK’s cyber minister, Liz Lloyd, noted the incident had "limited" impact on emergency services, yet the near‑miss raises questions about the adequacy of current resilience standards. In the EU, the European Commission’s Digital Services Act is being scrutinised for its enforcement mechanisms, while the U.S. Federal Communications Commission is considering proposals to classify major cloud platforms as essential communications services. Meanwhile, industry bodies such as the Cloud Infrastructure Providers Association are pushing for voluntary best‑practice frameworks, including mandatory multi‑region replication and automated rollback capabilities, to mitigate future systemic shocks.

key_facts: The outage affected more than 70 countries and over 430 million users of Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft traced the failure to a network capacity upgrade mis‑configuration, not a cyber‑attack.
Critical institutions impacted included the Japanese government, the Philippines Supreme Court, the UK NHS, and North American rail and hospital systems.
Recovery was gradual, with partial restoration reported by Friday morning and broader improvements by early afternoon.
Microsoft has not provided an exact ETA for full service recovery and will release a post‑incident report after internal review.
implications: Heightened awareness of single‑vendor risk among governments and enterprises, prompting calls for diversified cloud strategies.
Potential new regulatory classifications for cloud services as essential infrastructure, leading to stricter compliance requirements.
Increased investment in redundancy, failover and disaster‑recovery solutions across both public and private sectors.
items.outlook: In the months ahead, organisations are expected to accelerate adoption of multi‑cloud and edge‑computing architectures to hedge against similar disruptions. Policymakers are likely to introduce guidelines that mandate minimum uptime and transparency for providers of digital essential services. Microsoft, for its part, will face scrutiny over its incident‑response timelines and will need to demonstrate robust testing of upgrade procedures to restore user confidence.
items.fulltext:
Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
- Published
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.
Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.
By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
- Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? 
  - Published7 hours ago
- Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world 
  - Published8 hours ago
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".
His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".
Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.
"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.
"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.
'Encouraging recovery signals'
Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

items.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
items.tldr: Microsoft’s global outage, now over 20 hours, is a technical capacity‑upgrade failure that threatens email delivery and critical services. The incident highlights the fragility of cloud‑based communications and raises concerns about regulatory oversight of digital infrastructure.
items.background: On the evening of 13 Nov 2026, Microsoft reported a worldwide disruption of core 365 services—Outlook, Teams, Copilot and related AI tools. The failure, traced to a network capacity upgrade, has left schools, hospitals, courts and governments unable to send or receive email reliably. Microsoft has confirmed the issue is not a cyber‑attack, but a cascading server overload that is proving difficult to contain. The outage is already being described by industry veterans as the most disruptive business‑email failure in recent memory, with over 430 million users potentially affected.

analysis.heading: Technical Root Cause
analysis.content: Microsoft attributes the prolonged downtime to an earlier network‑capacity upgrade that overwhelmed the secure‑connection layer of its server cluster. According to Professor James Ferryman (University of Reading), this layer, which establishes SSL‑protected links, becomes a bottleneck when millions of devices attempt to reconnect simultaneously. The failure follows a classic “snowball” pattern: one server drops, traffic is rerouted to the next, and the surge of reconnection attempts compounds the load, creating a feedback loop that prevents a swift restart. The company’s statement that the underlying issue is “addressed” suggests a partial fix, but the residual load and the need for a phased re‑establishment of services explain the extended timeline.

analysis.heading: Operational Impact
analysis.content: The outage’s reach is broad and multi‑sector. Educational institutions report missing class communications, healthcare networks in Toronto and the UK face delayed patient correspondence, and judicial systems from Los Angeles to Texas warn of slowed case processing. Microsoft’s warning of “intermittent access issues” and a 48‑hour timeout window means many critical emails may be delayed or never reach their destination, jeopardising time‑sensitive workflows. The impact is amplified by the reliance on Microsoft 365 for verification in financial transactions, account recovery, and appointment scheduling, creating a ripple effect across finance, logistics and public services.

analysis.heading: Strategic Implications
analysis.content: From a policy perspective, the incident underscores the systemic risk posed by a single vendor’s cloud platform. Regulators are likely to revisit guidelines on service continuity, data‑resilience standards, and the need for redundancy in essential digital services. The editorial priorities—agentic AI, LLM, OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic—highlight the added complexity when AI‑driven tools (Copilot, ChatGPT integrations) also depend on the same infrastructure. In Myanmar, where connectivity is already fragile, the outage has further strained civic communication channels. The event also fuels debate on open‑source alternatives and the case for regulated “digital essential services” akin to utilities, potentially prompting new legislation on service‑level agreements and outage‑reporting obligations.

key_facts: Outage began late Thursday, 13 Nov 2026, and persisted for over 20 hours.
Microsoft cites a network capacity upgrade as the root cause, not a cyber‑attack.
At least 74 countries reported connectivity problems; services include Outlook, Teams and Copilot.
Microsoft extended email timeout to 48 hours to protect delayed messages.
More than 430 million Microsoft 365 users are potentially affected worldwide.
implications: Critical sectors (healthcare, education, justice) face operational delays and potential safety risks.
Regulatory scrutiny on cloud‑service providers is likely to increase, prompting new resilience standards.
Enterprises may accelerate diversification away from single‑vendor ecosystems or invest in redundant backup communications.
items.outlook: Recovery is progressing, with email queues reported as "significantly reduced" and approaching normal levels. However, intermittent issues are expected for several more days. Microsoft’s phased re‑launch strategy, combined with heightened regulatory attention, will shape how organisations mitigate future single‑point‑of‑failure risks. The incident also serves as a cautionary tale for the rapid adoption of AI services that rely on the same underlying infrastructure.

items.fulltext:
Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
- Published
A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world.
Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced.
Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.
From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.
"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.
Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive?
Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
Why has it taken so long to fix?
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.
Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.
